names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a pit beneath the earth.

insights.title: A textbook for the young
insights.body: The opening verses work like a title page, piling up words for wisdom, instruction, understanding and discretion (1:2-6). The book is aimed at the simple and the young man, but also at the wise, who can still increase in learning (1:5). In Israel, as in Egypt and Mesopotamia, such teaching was probably used at home, at court and in scribal training.

insights.title: Mashal, more than a proverb
insights.body: The Hebrew word for proverb, mashal, comes from a root meaning to be like or to compare. It covers short sayings, parables, taunt songs and riddles (1:6). A mashal invites the hearer to see one thing in the light of another, which is why so many proverbs are tiny comparisons.

insights.title: The fear of Yahweh
insights.body: The motto of the book is "The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge" (1:7), repeated near the end of the first section (9:10). The Hebrew for beginning, reshit, can mean both starting point and chief part. Fear here is reverent awe and loyalty toward God, not terror; it is where wisdom starts and what it never outgrows.

insights.title: Mother and father
insights.body: The son is told to listen to his father's instruction and his mother's teaching (1:8). The word for teaching is torah, the same word used for God's law. Proverbs regularly gives the mother an equal voice in instruction, and the book ends with a mother's words to her royal son.

insights.title: Swift to shed blood
insights.body: The gang's invitation is to easy money through violence, with all sharing one purse (1:13-14). The father answers that their feet run to evil and hurry to shed blood (1:16). Paul strings this line, together with Isaiah's parallel, into his chain of verses showing that all have sinned.

insights.title: The trap springs on the trapper
insights.body: A bird will not walk into a net it sees being spread (1:17), but these men set an ambush that ends up catching themselves (1:18). This is one of the book's favourite patterns: wrongdoing carries its own penalty, so that people eat of the fruit of their own way (1:31).

insights.title: Lady Wisdom speaks
insights.body: Wisdom is pictured as a woman calling in the streets, squares and city gates (1:20-21), the busiest public places. She sounds like a prophet, with her how long and her promise to pour out her spirit (1:22-23). This personified Wisdom returns in chapters 8 and 9 and later shapes how the New Testament speaks about Christ.

insights.title: When it is too late
insights.body: Wisdom says that those who ignored her will one day call and find no answer (1:28). Is this a statement about God's patience running out, or about how refusing wisdom slowly makes a person unable to receive it? |

1.summary: The book states its purpose, names the fear of Yahweh as the beginning of knowledge, warns a son against a violent gang, and lets Wisdom herself shout a warning in the streets.
1.lookfor: Watch for the list of people the book is written for, the two voices competing for the young man's attention, and how Wisdom speaks in public places.

insights.title: One long sentence
insights.body: In Hebrew the chapter is built like a single extended argument: if you receive, if you call, if you seek (2:1-4), then you will understand (2:5, 2:9), wisdom will deliver you (2:12, 2:16), and you will walk in the right way (2:20). Some scholars note it has 22 verses, the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet, perhaps as a teaching device. |

insights.title: Hidden treasure
insights.body: Seeking wisdom like silver and hidden treasures (2:4) recalls the mining described in Job, where men tunnel deep into the earth for ore. In a land without banks, people also buried valuables. The search is meant to take effort and desire.

insights.title: Seeking and receiving
insights.body: The son is told to call out and dig for wisdom, yet the very next line says Yahweh gives wisdom (2:6). Proverbs holds both together: wisdom is a gift from God, and it comes to those who want it badly enough to look.

insights.title: The strange woman
insights.body: The woman of 2:16 is called zarah and nokriyah, literally strange and foreign. The words can mean an outsider to the family, another man's wife or a foreigner. She is a real danger to young men in Proverbs, and she also becomes the opposite figure to Lady Wisdom.

insights.title: A broken covenant
insights.body: The seductress forsakes the friend of her youth and forgets the covenant of her God (2:17). Marriage is described here as a covenant made before God, a theme Malachi later develops when he calls a wife the wife of your covenant.

insights.title: Departed spirits
insights.body: Her paths lead to the rephaim (2:18), translated by WEB as departed spirits. The word is used for the shades of the dead and also for an ancient people of giants. Here it pictures her house as an entrance to the underworld.

insights.title: Who inherits the land
insights.body: The chapter closes with language from Israel's covenant: the upright will dwell in the land, while the wicked are rooted out (2:21-22). Psalm 37 says the same, and Jesus echoes it when he says the gentle will inherit the earth.

2.summary: The father promises that whoever searches for wisdom like buried treasure will find the knowledge of God and be kept from evil men and from the seductive stranger.
2.lookfor: Notice the chain of ifs and thens, how the search for wisdom turns out to be God's gift, and the two dangers wisdom guards against.

insights.title: Kindness and truth
insights.body: The pair in 3:3 is hesed and emet, the covenant love and faithfulness that God shows Israel. The son is to bind them around his neck and write them on his heart, language that echoes how Israel was told to keep God's words close.

insights.title: Trust with all your heart
insights.body: "Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don't lean on your own understanding" (3:5) is one of the best loved verses in the book. It does not reject thinking, since the whole book trains the mind; it warns against treating one's own judgment as final. He will make your paths straight can mean smooth and direct as well as morally upright (3:6).

insights.title: Discipline as love
insights.body: The father says Yahweh reproves the one he loves, as a father the son he delights in (3:11-12). Hebrews quotes this from the Greek translation to encourage persecuted believers to see hardship as training by a loving Father.

insights.title: The tree of life
insights.body: Wisdom is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her (3:18). The phrase recalls the tree in Eden that humanity lost, and Proverbs uses it four times. Revelation brings it back as the reward of those who overcome.

insights.title: Wisdom in creation
insights.body: By wisdom Yahweh founded the earth (3:19). The same wisdom that orders the world is offered to the son for ordering his life. This link between creation and daily conduct is the foundation of biblical wisdom, and it is developed fully in chapter 8.

insights.title: Payday today
insights.body: Don't tell a neighbour to come back tomorrow when you have what he is owed now (3:27-28). For day labourers and the poor, a delayed payment could mean a hungry night. The law of Moses required wages to be paid before sunset.

insights.title: Grace to the humble
insights.body: He mocks the mockers but gives grace to the humble (3:34). James and Peter both quote this verse in its Greek form, "God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble."

insights.title: Barns and blessing
insights.body: Honouring Yahweh with first fruits is followed by the promise of full barns (3:9-10). How should this promise be read alongside Job and Ecclesiastes, which know that the faithful sometimes suffer loss?

3.summary: The father urges loyalty and trust in Yahweh, praises wisdom as more precious than rubies and as the tree of life, and gives practical rules for treating neighbours well.
3.lookfor: Look for the promises attached to each command, the picture of wisdom at creation, and the series of don'ts toward neighbours at the end.

insights.title: Three generations
insights.body: The father remembers being a tender only child, taught by his own father (4:3-4). Wisdom here is a family inheritance handed down rather than invented. Jewish tradition, reading the book as Solomon's, saw David's teaching behind these lines.

insights.title: Get wisdom
insights.body: The command in 4:5 and 4:7 uses the Hebrew verb qanah, to acquire or buy. Wisdom is worth more than any purchase: though it costs all your possessions, get understanding. The same verb appears when Wisdom says Yahweh possessed her (8:22).

insights.title: A garland and a crown
insights.body: Wisdom will give a garland of grace and a crown of splendour (4:9). In the ancient world wreaths were worn at feasts and weddings and crowns marked honour. Wisdom makes a person beautiful and honoured, as the father's teaching was earlier called a garland (1:9).

insights.title: Two ways
insights.body: The chapter contrasts the path of the righteous, like dawn growing to full day (4:18), with the way of the wicked, so dark that they don't know what they stumble over (4:19). The image of two ways runs through the Psalms and into Jesus' words about the narrow and broad roads.

insights.title: Keep your heart
insights.body: "Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life" (4:23). In Hebrew thought the heart, lev, is less the seat of feelings than the centre of thinking, choosing and character. Jesus likewise says that evil words and deeds come out of the heart.

insights.title: Heart, mouth, eyes, feet
insights.body: The final verses move through the whole person: heart (4:23), mouth and lips (4:24), eyes (4:25) and feet (4:26-27). Wisdom is not only ideas; it governs what we love, say, look at and where we go.

insights.title: Restless wickedness
insights.body: The wicked cannot sleep until they have done harm (4:16). The father pictures evil as an addiction that eats the bread of wickedness and drinks the wine of violence (4:17). The warning is aimed at a young man who might be drawn in by such company.

4.summary: A father passes on what his own father taught him: get wisdom whatever it costs, keep off the path of the wicked, and guard the heart from which life flows.
4.lookfor: Notice the three generations in the opening, the contrast of light and darkness on the two paths, and the parts of the body named at the end.

insights.title: Speaking plainly to young men
insights.body: Proverbs 5 to 7 return again and again to sexual temptation. The audience is young men about to marry and enter public life, and the father is blunt about the costs of adultery: wealth, honour, health and years. The book treats faithfulness as a matter of wisdom as well as morality.

insights.title: Honey and wormwood
insights.body: Her lips drip honey and her speech is smoother than oil (5:3), but in the end she is as bitter as wormwood (5:4). Wormwood is a bitter plant (Artemisia) that the Bible uses as a picture of sorrow and poison.

insights.title: Regret in public
insights.body: The man who ignored his teachers ends up groaning and saying "How I have hated instruction" (5:12). He comes to ruin among the gathered assembly (5:14), probably meaning public disgrace before the community that judged such cases.

insights.title: Your own cistern
insights.body: "Drink water out of your own cistern" (5:15). In a dry land, every household guarded its cistern and well, and water from a private spring was precious. The image pictures marital love as a source of life to be kept, not shared with strangers (5:16-17).

insights.title: Joy in the wife of your youth
insights.body: Proverbs does not only forbid; it commends delight. The son is told to rejoice in his wife and be captivated by her love (5:18-19). The Hebrew word for captivated, shagah, is the same used for the man who goes astray (5:23), a deliberate play on words.

insights.title: Seen by Yahweh
insights.body: The ways of man are before Yahweh's eyes (5:21). What happens in secret is never private from God. The chapter joins this to the book's other conviction, that sin becomes its own trap: the cords of his sin hold him firmly (5:22).

insights.title: The cost of folly
insights.body: The chapter ends not with a dramatic punishment but with a man who dies for lack of instruction (5:23). What does it suggest that the root problem is pictured as a refusal to be taught rather than a lack of willpower?

5.summary: The father warns his son that the adulteress's sweet words lead to death and ruin, and urges him instead to find joy and delight in his own wife.
5.lookfor: Watch for the contrast between honey and wormwood, the water imagery in the middle of the chapter, and the regret of the man who would not listen.

insights.title: Striking hands
insights.body: To become collateral and strike hands in pledge (6:1) was to guarantee another person's debt with a handshake. If the borrower defaulted, the guarantor was liable. The father urges urgent humility to get released from the promise before it ruins him (6:3-5).

insights.title: Go to the ant
insights.body: The sluggard is sent to learn from the ant, which works without chief, overseer or ruler (6:7). Harvester ants in Israel gather and store grain, a sight familiar to farmers. The point is self-motivated foresight, not just hard work.

insights.title: A little sleep
insights.body: "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to sleep" (6:10) captures how laziness rarely feels like a decision. Poverty arrives like a robber or armed man (6:11), suddenly and without asking. The same lines return almost word for word later in the book.

insights.title: Winks and gestures
insights.body: The worthless person winks, signals with his feet and motions with his fingers (6:13). In a culture with oral agreements, secret gestures could signal a plot or mock a victim behind his back. Psalm 35 also complains of enemies who wink with the eye.

insights.title: Six things, yes seven
insights.body: The list of things Yahweh hates (6:16-19) uses a numerical pattern, six and then seven, also found in Amos and elsewhere in wisdom literature. The seventh, he who sows discord among brothers, is probably the climax. Haughty eyes come first, and most of the list is about body parts used for harm.

insights.title: The commandment is a lamp
insights.body: Binding the parents' words on the heart and neck (6:21) echoes Deuteronomy's command to keep God's words on hand and forehead. "The commandment is a lamp, and the law is light" (6:23) is close to Psalm 119's lamp to my feet.

insights.title: Thief and adulterer
insights.body: A starving thief is not despised, yet the law still makes him repay, and here sevenfold, perhaps meaning in full (6:30-31). Exodus sets lower restitution rates, so seven may be a figure for completeness. The adulterer, by contrast, faces a husband no gift can appease (6:34-35).

insights.title: Fire in the lap
insights.body: "Can a man scoop fire into his lap, and his clothes not be burned?" (6:27). Why might the father appeal to plain consequences here rather than simply to the command against adultery?

6.summary: The father warns against rash pledges and laziness, lists seven things Yahweh hates, and returns to the danger of adultery with an image of fire in the lap.
6.lookfor: Look for the ant, the six-and-seven list, and the comparison between a hungry thief and an adulterer.

insights.title: Wisdom as a sister
insights.body: The son is told to call wisdom his sister and understanding his relative (7:4). Sister was also a term of endearment for a beloved, as in the Song of Solomon. The father wants the son to have a close and loving relationship with wisdom before the other woman offers one.

insights.title: A view through the lattice
insights.body: The father looks out through a lattice (7:6), the wooden screen covering upper windows in ancient houses. The scene is told like a short story with a narrator, a naive young man, a setting at twilight (7:9) and a dialogue.

insights.title: Meat from the sacrifice
insights.body: The woman says she has peace offerings and has paid her vows today (7:14). Meat from a vow offering had to be eaten that day or the next, so she has a feast at home. She dresses up her invitation in religious language.

insights.title: Imported luxury
insights.body: Her bed has coloured linen from Egypt and is perfumed with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon (7:16-17). These were costly imports, and the same spices appear in the Song of Solomon. Here they belong to a seduction that ends in death.

insights.title: The husband away
insights.body: She says her husband has taken a bag of money on a long journey and won't be back until the full moon (7:19-20). This assures the young man there is no danger of being caught, and suggests a planned absence of some days at least.

insights.title: Void of understanding
insights.body: The young man is literally lacking heart (7:7), the Hebrew way of saying without sense. He is not wicked by intention, only simple, and that is the danger: he drifts down her street in the dark (7:8) without deciding much at all.

insights.title: Like an ox to slaughter
insights.body: Three images of animals close the story: an ox led to slaughter, a fool stepping into a noose, a bird rushing into a snare (7:22-23). An arrow through the liver, seen in the ancient world as a seat of life and emotion, shows what the young man does not see.

insights.title: A mighty army of the slain
insights.body: The woman has thrown down many (7:26) and her house is the way to Sheol (7:27). The final warning prepares for chapters 8 and 9, where Wisdom and Folly each call from the high places of the city and the reader must choose whose house to enter.

7.summary: The father describes watching from his window as a foolish young man is seduced at dusk by a married woman, and follows him like an ox to the slaughter.
7.lookfor: Notice the time of day, every detail of the woman's speech, and the comparisons to animals in the last part of the story.

insights.title: Speaking to everyone
insights.body: Unlike the stranger who lurks at corners in the dark, Wisdom stands openly at the crossroads and city gates (8:2-3) and calls to the sons of mankind (8:4). She speaks to all humanity, not only to Israel.

insights.title: By me kings reign
insights.body: Wisdom says rulers govern and decree justice through her (8:15-16). In the ancient world wisdom was the king's chief virtue, which is why Solomon asked God for it. Proverbs presents good government as an application of God's wisdom.

insights.title: Possessed or created
insights.body: Yahweh possessed me in the beginning (8:22) translates the Hebrew qanani. The verb can mean acquire, possess or create, and the Greek translation chose created. In the 4th century Arius used the verse to argue that the Son was a created being, and Athanasius and other defenders of the Council of Nicaea answered that it must be read differently, often of the Son's coming in the flesh.

insights.title: Born before the mountains
insights.body: Wisdom says she was born before the depths, springs and hills (8:24-25). The picture of God setting a circle on the deep and giving the sea its boundary (8:27-29) uses the ancient image of the world as dry land held safe from the waters.

insights.title: Craftsman or little child
insights.body: In 8:30 the Hebrew amon is uncertain. It may mean a master craftsman beside God, as WEB renders it, or a nursling, a little child playing before him. Both fit: one stresses Wisdom's role in shaping the world, the other her delight in it. |

insights.title: Wisdom and the Word
insights.body: Early Christians heard this chapter behind John's Word who was with God in the beginning and through whom all things were made, and behind Paul calling Christ the wisdom of God. Jewish tradition, by contrast, identified Wisdom with the Torah, which a well-known midrash on Genesis pictures as the blueprint God consulted when he made the world.

insights.title: Delight with the sons of men
insights.body: Wisdom says she was a delight to God day by day, rejoicing in his world, and her delight was with the sons of men (8:30-31). The creation passage ends not with power but with joy, and with humanity as the object of Wisdom's pleasure.

insights.title: Finds life, loves death
insights.body: "Whoever finds me, finds life" while all who hate wisdom love death (8:35-36). Is this a promise about long life, a statement about what kind of life is truly life, or both?

8.summary: Wisdom calls to all people from the city gates, describes her worth and authority over kings, and tells how she was with Yahweh before the world began, delighting in his creation.
8.lookfor: Watch for where Wisdom stands, what she says she gives to those who love her, and her account of being present at creation.

insights.title: Seven pillars
insights.body: Wisdom's house has seven pillars (9:1). Large ancient houses and public buildings had courtyards surrounded by pillars. Seven suggests completeness. Scholars debate whether the image comes from temple or palace design or is simply symbolic.

insights.title: Mixed wine
insights.body: Wisdom has mixed her wine (9:2, 9:5). Ancient wine was often mixed with water or spices before serving, and mixing it was part of preparing a feast. Her table is generous, with meat, bread and wine.

insights.title: Twin invitations
insights.body: Both women call from the high places of the city and say exactly the same words: "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here" (9:4, 9:16). The reader must choose not between a good and an obviously bad voice, but between two attractive offers.

insights.title: Teachable or not
insights.body: The middle verses (9:7-12) describe the difference between a mocker, who hates correction, and a wise man, who loves it and grows wiser. The proof of wisdom is not what one knows but how one takes reproof.

insights.title: The Holy One
insights.body: "The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of wisdom. The knowledge of the Holy One is understanding" (9:10). This bookends 1:7 and closes the first section of Proverbs. In Hebrew Holy One is plural, probably a plural of majesty, as in other titles for God.

insights.title: Stolen water is sweet
insights.body: Folly offers only water and bread, not meat and wine, and its attraction is that it is stolen and secret (9:17). Her guests do not know they are already in the depths of Sheol (9:18).

insights.title: Come, eat my bread
insights.body: Wisdom's invitation to eat bread and drink wine (9:5) has been echoed in Isaiah's call to come and buy without money and in Jesus' feeding and his words about the bread of life. Christian readers have also heard it at the Lord's table.

insights.title: Which house?
insights.body: The first nine chapters end with a choice of houses. The rest of Proverbs, the short sayings, can be read as what life in Wisdom's house looks like day by day.

9.summary: Wisdom builds her house and invites the simple to her feast, Folly calls from her doorway with stolen water, and in between come sayings about mockers and the wise.
9.lookfor: Compare the two invitations line by line, and notice how the short sayings in the middle sit between the two banquets.

insights.title: A new kind of writing
insights.body: With a fresh heading (10:1) the book changes from long speeches to single sayings, most only two lines long. Each can stand alone, so the collection is meant to be read slowly, a few at a time, rather than as an argument. Some scholars find small clusters grouped by theme or catchword.

insights.title: The number of Solomon
insights.body: The section from 10:1 to 22:16 contains 375 verses. The letters of Solomon's name in Hebrew have the numerical value 375, and many scholars think this is deliberate, a kind of signature on the collection.

insights.title: Antithetic parallelism
insights.body: Hebrew poetry pairs lines. In chapters 10 to 15 the second line usually states the opposite of the first, joined by but. The contrast forces a choice: there is a wise way and a foolish way, with very little middle ground.

insights.title: Of blessed memory
insights.body: The memory of the righteous is blessed, but the name of the wicked will rot (10:7). Jews still speak of the dead as of blessed memory, a phrase drawn from this verse. Since much of the Old Testament says little about life after death, a good name that lived on in the community mattered greatly.

insights.title: Love covers
insights.body: "Hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all wrongs" (10:12). Peter quotes it in the form love covers a multitude of sins, and James uses the same phrase. Covering here means not exposing or stirring up, rather than pretending wrong did not happen.

insights.title: Repeated lines
insights.body: The second half of 10:6 reappears in 10:11, and the second half of 10:8 in 10:10. Such repeats show how sayings circulated: a well-known line could be attached to different openings. Readers can compare what each pairing teaches.

insights.title: Vinegar and smoke
insights.body: A lazy messenger is as vinegar to the teeth and smoke to the eyes for whoever sends him (10:26). The comparison is from everyday life: small, sharp irritations. In a world without post, a slow or unreliable messenger could do real damage.

insights.title: Wealth and blessing
insights.body: The chapter says both that diligent hands bring wealth (10:4) and that Yahweh's blessing brings it (10:22). How do these two claims fit together, and what does adding no trouble to it suggest about wealth gained other ways?

10.summary: The main collection of Solomon's proverbs begins with a stream of two-line sayings contrasting the wise and the foolish, the diligent and the lazy, and the righteous and the wicked, especially in how they speak.
10.lookfor: Notice the word but in the middle of almost every verse, and count how many sayings are about the mouth, lips and tongue.

insights.title: Honest weights
insights.body: Before coins, payment was weighed out in silver on a hand-held balance using stone weights. Archaeologists have found many such weights in Israel, some marked with their value, and not all weigh what they claim. A false balance is an abomination to Yahweh (11:1), as the law and the prophets also say.

insights.title: Pride before shame
insights.body: When pride comes, then comes shame, but with humility comes wisdom (11:2). In Hebrew the words for pride and shame rhyme (zadon and qalon), making the saying easy to remember. The idea returns in the better-known pride goes before destruction.

insights.title: Good for the city
insights.body: The righteous are not only private individuals: when it goes well with them the city rejoices (11:10), and their blessing exalts it (11:11). Wise and just people make a whole community healthier, while wicked mouths can overthrow it.

insights.title: A gold nose ring
insights.body: "Like a gold ring in a pig's snout, is a beautiful woman who lacks discretion" (11:22). Nose rings were common jewellery for women, as when Abraham's servant gave one to Rebekah. To Israelites pigs were unclean, so the image is deliberately jarring: beauty wasted on a setting unworthy of it.

insights.title: The generous get more
insights.body: One who scatters gains more, and he who waters shall be watered (11:24-25). The saying runs against simple economic logic. People curse whoever hoards grain in a famine to push the price up, but bless the one who sells (11:26).

insights.title: Wins souls
insights.body: He who is wise wins souls (11:30) is literally takes lives, a Hebrew phrase that usually means to kill. Here it is taken positively to mean draws people in or wins them over; the Greek translation reads it differently, as violence taking lives. The tree of life in the first line shows the positive sense.

insights.title: How much more
insights.body: The chapter ends: if the righteous are repaid on earth, how much more the wicked and the sinner (11:31). Peter quotes the Greek form of this verse: "If it is hard for the righteous to be saved, what will happen to the ungodly and the sinner?"

insights.title: Trust in riches
insights.body: "He who trusts in his riches will fall" (11:28). The book often praises wealth honestly gained. Where is the line between having wealth and trusting in it?

11.summary: The sayings continue with honest business, pride and humility, the effect of the righteous on their city, generosity and greed, and how both righteous and wicked receive what their ways deserve.
11.lookfor: Watch for the city and the marketplace, the comparison of a beautiful woman to a pig's ring, and the sayings about giving and withholding.

insights.title: Loving correction
insights.body: The chapter opens bluntly: whoever hates reproof is stupid (12:1). The Hebrew word, ba'ar, is related to the word for cattle; such a person is brutish, like an animal without understanding. Being teachable is the first mark of wisdom.

insights.title: A worthy woman
insights.body: A worthy woman is her husband's crown (12:4). The phrase is eshet chayil, a woman of strength or valour, the same phrase that heads the poem about the capable wife in chapter 31.

insights.title: Kindness to animals
insights.body: A righteous man respects the life of his animal (12:10), literally knows its soul. The law of Moses included rest for animals on the Sabbath and forbade muzzling an ox while it threshed. In a farming society, cruelty to working animals was common and easy.

insights.title: Fantasies or fields
insights.body: He who tills his land shall have plenty, but he who chases fantasies is void of understanding (12:11). The Hebrew word for fantasies means empty things; the warning is against get-rich-quick schemes in place of steady work.

insights.title: Slow to take offence
insights.body: A fool shows his annoyance the same day, but the prudent overlooks an insult (12:16). Wisdom literature consistently values restraint over quick reaction, and James echoes it with slow to speak and slow to anger.

insights.title: Swords and healing
insights.body: Rash speech pierces like a sword, but the tongue of the wise heals (12:18). A kind word makes an anxious heart glad (12:25). The book treats speech as one of the most powerful forces for good or harm in daily life.

insights.title: Roasting the game
insights.body: The slothful man doesn't roast his game (12:27). The Hebrew is unusual and may mean he does not bother to cook what he caught or, as some suggest, never catches anything at all. Either way, laziness wastes what effort or opportunity has provided.

insights.title: No death in its path
insights.body: The chapter ends: in the way of righteousness is life, and in its path there is no death (12:28). Many scholars think this verse points beyond long life toward hope over death itself, while others read it as a strong way of saying the righteous way is fully life-giving. Which reading seems more natural?

12.summary: These sayings contrast the man who loves correction with the one who hates it, and look at work, honest speech, the use of words to wound or heal, and kindness even to animals.
12.lookfor: Look for the sayings about the tongue as sword or healer, and the small details of farm life: animals, fields and game.

insights.title: Guarding the mouth
insights.body: He who guards his mouth guards his soul (13:3). The word for soul, nefesh, also means life or throat. Careless words can cost a person his very life.

insights.title: Rich and poor pretenders
insights.body: Some pretend to be rich and have nothing, others pretend to be poor and have great wealth (13:7). Appearances in money matters deceive. The next verse adds that riches may ransom a life, but the poor at least receive no threats (13:8).

insights.title: Hope deferred
insights.body: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick, but when longing is fulfilled, it is a tree of life" (13:12). Proverbs recognises the emotional cost of waiting. The tree of life appears again as an image of joy and renewal.

insights.title: Choose your company
insights.body: One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm (13:20). The first chapter already warned against falling in with the wrong crowd, and Paul cites a Greek saying that bad company corrupts good morals.

insights.title: Not all poverty is laziness
insights.body: Some sayings tie poverty to laziness, but 13:23 says the poor man's field may yield plenty and injustice sweeps it away. Proverbs knows that oppression as well as sloth makes people poor, and readers should not take any single saying as the whole picture.

insights.title: The rod
insights.body: One who spares the rod hates his son (13:24). Physical discipline was normal in the ancient world, and the saying stresses that loving parents do not leave children uncorrected. Christians and Jews today differ over whether the rod should be taken literally, and Paul adds that fathers must not provoke children to wrath.

insights.title: An inheritance for grandchildren
insights.body: A good man leaves an inheritance to his children's children (13:22). Wisdom thinks across generations, as the father in chapter 4 passed on his father's teaching. Land in Israel was meant to stay in the family as God's gift.

insights.title: The light and the lamp
insights.body: The righteous' light shines brightly, while the wicked's lamp is snuffed out (13:9). A burning lamp was a common picture of a family's continuing life. What might it mean for a person's life to give light?

13.summary: These sayings deal with listening to instruction, guarding the mouth, honest and dishonest wealth, hope and longing, the influence of companions, and disciplining children.
13.lookfor: Notice the sayings about hope, the different kinds of rich and poor, and the warning about the friends one keeps.

insights.title: Building and tearing down
insights.body: Every wise woman builds her house (14:1). The verse echoes Wisdom, who built her house in chapter 9, and Folly, whose house leads to death. A household's flourishing depends on the wisdom of those running it.

insights.title: A clean stable
insights.body: Where no oxen are, the crib is clean, but much increase comes by the strength of the ox (14:4). A farmer without oxen has no mess, but also no harvest. The saying works well beyond farming: anything fruitful brings untidiness with it.

insights.title: Hidden hearts
insights.body: The heart knows its own bitterness and joy, and no stranger shares in them (14:10). Even in laughter the heart may be sorrowful (14:13). Proverbs knows the limits of what others can see in us and what we can see in them.

insights.title: The way that seems right
insights.body: "There is a way which seems right to a man, but in the end it leads to death" (14:12). The same saying appears again word for word in 16:25. It sums up the danger of being wise in one's own eyes.

insights.title: Slow to anger
insights.body: He who is slow to anger has great understanding (14:29). Slow to anger, literally long of nostrils, is a phrase used of God himself in Exodus. Those who hold their temper reflect God's own character.

insights.title: The poor and their Maker
insights.body: "He who oppresses the poor shows contempt for his Maker, but he who is kind to the needy honors him" (14:31). Because the poor are made by God, how they are treated is how God is treated. Jesus says the same of the least of his brothers.

insights.title: Righteousness and the nation
insights.body: Righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a disgrace to any people (14:34). The saying applies to every people, not only Israel. Wisdom literature assumes a moral order built into the world that holds for all nations.

insights.title: A refuge in death
insights.body: In death, the righteous has a refuge (14:32). Some scholars follow the Greek translation and read in his integrity instead, a difference of two letters in Hebrew. If the traditional Hebrew is right, what hope might it suggest about death?

14.summary: The sayings contrast the wise woman who builds her house with the fool who tears it down, and cover honest witness, the hidden heart, the way that seems right, anger, and care for the poor.
14.lookfor: Look for the ox in the stable, the sayings about the heart's private joys and sorrows, and the link between how we treat the poor and how we treat God.

names.name: Abaddon
names.gloss: A Hebrew name for the place of the dead, meaning destruction, paired with Sheol.

insights.title: A gentle answer
insights.body: "A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger" (15:1). The chapter opens and closes with speech: a soft reply calms anger, and a word at the right time brings joy (15:23). The tongue can give life like a tree (15:4).

insights.title: Sheol and Abaddon
insights.body: Abaddon (15:11) means destruction and is a poetic name for the realm of the dead. If even the underworld lies open before Yahweh, how much more the human heart. Revelation later gives Abaddon as the Hebrew name of the angel of the abyss.

insights.title: Sacrifice and prayer
insights.body: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to Yahweh, but the prayer of the upright delights him (15:8). Proverbs agrees with the prophets that worship without justice and obedience is empty. Jesus likewise says to be reconciled first and then offer the gift.

insights.title: Herbs or a fattened calf
insights.body: "Better is a dinner of herbs, where love is, than a fattened calf with hatred" (15:17). For most Israelites meat was a rare luxury, eaten at feasts, while daily meals were bread, vegetables and legumes. A fattened calf was festival food, as in the parable of the prodigal son.

insights.title: Better than
insights.body: Sayings in the form better is X than Y (15:16-17) are common in wisdom literature, including Egyptian teaching. They rank goods rather than praising one and condemning another. Here peace, love and the fear of Yahweh outrank wealth.

insights.title: The widow's boundary
insights.body: Yahweh keeps the widow's borders intact (15:25). Fields were marked by boundary stones, and moving them was an easy way to steal land from those without protectors. The law forbade it, and Proverbs names God as the widow's defender.

insights.title: Humility before honour
insights.body: The chapter ends with the fear of Yahweh and the saying that humility comes before honour (15:33). This verse is often seen as a hinge, leading into a cluster of sayings that name Yahweh in nearly every verse at the start of chapter 16.

insights.title: Weighing answers
insights.body: The heart of the righteous weighs answers, while the mouth of the wicked gushes out evil (15:28). What would change in a conversation if one weighed answers before speaking?

15.summary: These sayings focus on gentle and harsh words, God's watchful eye, sincere and empty worship, contentment with little, and the value of counsel and correction.
15.lookfor: Look for the better-than sayings, the contrast between the sacrifice of the wicked and the prayer of the upright, and the word spoken at the right time.

insights.title: Yahweh at the centre
insights.body: In 16:1-9 Yahweh is named in nearly every verse, which is unusual in the sayings collection. These verses sit close to the middle of Solomon's proverbs, and many scholars think the placing is deliberate: human wisdom works within God's rule.

insights.title: We plan, God directs
insights.body: "A man's heart plans his course, but Yahweh directs his steps" (16:9), and the same idea opens the chapter (16:1). Proverbs commends planning, but never as though the future were under human control. James makes the same point about merchants making plans for a year.

insights.title: Mercy and truth atone
insights.body: By mercy and truth iniquity is atoned for (16:6). The pair is hesed and emet again, covenant love and faithfulness. The verse does not dismiss sacrifice, but it echoes the prophets' insistence that God looks for faithfulness and love.

insights.title: The king's face
insights.body: The king's wrath is a messenger of death, but the light of his face is life and his favour like spring rain (16:14-15). The late spring rains before harvest were vital to the crops. Courtiers lived or died by the king's mood, and the wise knew how to calm it.

insights.title: Before a fall
insights.body: "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (16:18). This is one of the most quoted verses in the book, often shortened in English to pride comes before a fall. Its partner, better to be lowly with the poor than share plunder with the proud, follows (16:19).

insights.title: A crown of gray hair
insights.body: Gray hair is a crown of glory (16:31). In Israel old age was honoured, and the law told the young to rise before the elderly. The proverb assumes that a long life usually comes from walking in righteousness, though other passages admit exceptions.

insights.title: Ruling one's spirit
insights.body: One who is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and one who rules his spirit than he who takes a city (16:32). Self-mastery is ranked above military glory. Paul lists self-control as a fruit of the Spirit.

insights.title: The lot in the lap
insights.body: "The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from Yahweh" (16:33). Israel used lots to divide land, choose officials and settle questions, and the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias. What looks like chance is under God's rule.

16.summary: These sayings set human plans beside God's sovereignty, describe the king's justice and power, and praise humility, self-control and gracious speech.
16.lookfor: Notice how often Yahweh is named in the first nine verses, then the group of sayings about kings, and the final verse about the lot.

insights.title: The refiner's fire
insights.body: Silver and gold are tested in the refining pot and furnace, but Yahweh tests hearts (17:3). Ancient refiners heated ore until impurities rose and could be skimmed off. The prophets use the same picture for God purifying his people.

insights.title: Observing a bribe
insights.body: A bribe is like a precious stone to the giver, opening doors wherever he turns (17:8). Proverbs often describes how the world works without approving it; a few verses later it condemns the man who takes a bribe in secret to pervert justice (17:23).

insights.title: A bear robbed of her cubs
insights.body: Better to meet a mother bear robbed of her cubs than a fool in his folly (17:12). Syrian brown bears lived in Israel in biblical times, and a she-bear defending her young was a byword for fury, used by Hushai and Hosea.

insights.title: Breaching a dam
insights.body: The beginning of strife is like breaching a dam (17:14). A small crack in an earth dam or cistern wall quickly becomes a flood. The advice is to stop a quarrel early, before it becomes unstoppable.

insights.title: Covering an offence
insights.body: He who covers an offence promotes love, but he who repeats a matter separates friends (17:9). This continues the thought that love covers all wrongs. Passing on someone's fault, even if true, destroys friendships.

insights.title: Born for adversity
insights.body: "A friend loves at all times; and a brother is born for adversity" (17:17). The two lines may be parallel, so that a true friend becomes a brother in hard times. Either way, loyalty is proved in trouble, not in good times.

insights.title: Grief of a parent
insights.body: Three verses speak of the grief a foolish son brings his father and mother (17:21, 17:25). Proverbs was taught by parents who knew that teaching does not guarantee the outcome. The sayings carry the pain of watching a child go astray.

insights.title: Silence that looks wise
insights.body: Even a fool who keeps silent is counted wise (17:28). Is this simple advice to say less, or a sharper comment on how easily silence is mistaken for wisdom?

17.summary: These sayings praise peace over plenty, warn against bribery and gossip, prize loyal friendship and quiet speech, and describe the grief a foolish child brings.
17.lookfor: Look for the bear robbed of her cubs, the burst dam, and the sayings about friends and brothers.

insights.title: Loving one's own opinion
insights.body: A fool has no delight in understanding, only in revealing his own opinion (18:2). Answering before hearing is folly and shame (18:13). The first sign of wisdom in Proverbs is not having answers but being willing to listen.

insights.title: Dainty morsels
insights.body: The words of a gossip are like dainty morsels that go down into the innermost parts (18:8). Gossip is pictured as a tasty snack, hard to resist and quickly swallowed, which stays inside the hearer. The same saying appears again in chapter 26.

insights.title: Two strongholds
insights.body: "Yahweh's name is a strong tower: the righteous run to him, and are safe" (18:10). The next verse sets beside it the rich man's wealth, a strong city like an unscalable wall in his own imagination (18:11). Placed side by side, the sayings ask where a person really runs for safety.

insights.title: Hearing both sides
insights.body: He who pleads his cause first seems right until another comes and questions him (18:17). This is the procedure of the city gate, where elders heard disputes. The law required more than one witness, and a fair judge heard both sides before deciding.

insights.title: A gift makes room
insights.body: A man's gift makes room for him and brings him before great men (18:16). Gifts opened doors in ancient society, as when Jacob sent gifts ahead to Esau. The saying observes this without saying whether it is right; elsewhere Proverbs warns that gifts can become bribes.

insights.title: Death and life in the tongue
insights.body: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue" (18:21). In Hebrew, power is literally hand: the tongue holds life and death in its grip. Those who love using it will eat its fruit, for good or ill.

insights.title: Finding a wife
insights.body: Whoever finds a wife finds a good thing and obtains favour from Yahweh (18:22). The wording recalls Genesis, where it is not good for the man to be alone. The Greek translation adds lines against sending away a good wife and keeping an adulteress, which are not in the Hebrew.

insights.title: Closer than a brother
insights.body: A man of many companions may be ruined, but there is a friend who sticks closer than a brother (18:24). The Hebrew contrasts shallow companions with true friendship. Many Christian readers have heard in it a description of Christ, who calls his disciples friends.

18.summary: These sayings contrast the isolated fool who loves his own opinion with those who listen first, and speak of the power of the tongue, the strong tower of Yahweh's name, and true friendship.
18.lookfor: Compare the strong tower in 18:10 with the strong city in 18:11, and notice how many sayings are about listening and speaking.

insights.title: Fair-weather friends
insights.body: Wealth adds many friends, but the poor man's relatives shun him and his friends avoid him (19:4, 19:6-7). Proverbs records this coldly, without approving it. The pleading poor man in 19:7 is a picture of real loneliness.

insights.title: Zeal without knowledge
insights.body: It isn't good to have zeal without knowledge (19:2). Energy without understanding leads people to rush and miss the way. Paul uses the same contrast of zeal and knowledge when he speaks about his own people.

insights.title: Glory in overlooking
insights.body: It is a man's glory to overlook an offence (19:11). In an honour culture, letting a wrong go could look weak. Proverbs says the opposite: patience and forgiveness are a kind of glory.

insights.title: A dripping roof
insights.body: A wife's quarrels are a continual dripping (19:13). Flat roofs of packed earth and branches leaked during the winter rains, and the steady drip was hard to escape. The same image returns in chapter 27, alongside other sayings about a contentious spouse.

insights.title: Lending to Yahweh
insights.body: "He who has pity on the poor lends to Yahweh; he will reward him" (19:17). The Hebrew word for lends is the ordinary word for making a loan. God takes on the debt himself, so that no kindness to the poor goes unpaid.

insights.title: The sluggard's dish
insights.body: The sluggard buries his hand in the dish and won't even bring it back to his mouth (19:24). People ate from a shared bowl, using bread or the hand. The cartoon of a man too lazy to feed himself makes laziness laughable as well as dangerous.

insights.title: Yahweh's counsel prevails
insights.body: There are many plans in a man's heart, but Yahweh's counsel will prevail (19:21). The book's practical advice always sits under this conviction. Joseph's story is one long illustration: what others planned for evil, God meant for good.

insights.title: Discipline and hope
insights.body: Discipline your son, for there is hope (19:18). The second line warns parents not to let a child go his own way to destruction. What does it say about hope that discipline is presented as a sign of it?

19.summary: These sayings look at how poverty and wealth affect friendships, the value of patience and discipline, kindness to the poor as a loan to God, and the limits of human plans.
19.lookfor: Watch for the different kinds of friends, the dripping roof, and the comic picture of the sluggard at the table.

insights.title: Wine and beer
insights.body: Wine is a mocker, and beer is a brawler (20:1). The Hebrew shekar means fermented drink, which in the ancient Near East was often barley beer. Wine was a normal part of life and celebration in Israel, but Proverbs warns repeatedly against being led astray by it.

insights.title: Steps we cannot see
insights.body: A man's steps are from Yahweh; how then can man understand his way? (20:24). The proverbs are full of confident advice, yet this one admits that no one fully understands his own path. How might that humility change the way the rest of the advice is used?

insights.title: Who can say I am clean
insights.body: "Who can say, 'I have made my heart pure. I am clean and without sin?'" (20:9). The question expects the answer no one. Solomon's temple prayer says there is no one who doesn't sin, and John warns that those who say they have no sin deceive themselves.

insights.title: The haggling buyer
insights.body: "It's no good, it's no good," says the buyer, then goes off boasting of his bargain (20:14). Bargaining in the market was normal. Proverbs smiles at the buyer's double talk, but the point is that his words were not honest.

insights.title: A cloak as pledge
insights.body: Take the garment of one who guarantees a stranger's debt (20:16). A cloak was a common pledge for a loan. The law required a poor man's cloak to be returned by sunset because it was his blanket, but a fool who backs strangers' debts is fair game.

insights.title: Leave revenge to God
insights.body: Don't say I will pay back evil; wait for Yahweh, and he will save you (20:22). This is close to Paul's instruction to repay no one evil for evil and leave room for God's wrath. Wisdom restrains the urge for revenge.

insights.title: The lamp of Yahweh
insights.body: The spirit of man is Yahweh's lamp, searching all his innermost parts (20:27). The word for spirit here is neshamah, the breath of life God breathed into Adam. The human spirit, given by God, is the means by which a person is known through and through.

insights.title: Rash vows
insights.body: It is a snare to dedicate something rashly and think about the vow afterwards (20:25). Israel's story has tragic examples, most famously Jephthah. Ecclesiastes also warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.

20.summary: These sayings warn about drink, laziness, haggling and dishonest weights, rash vows and revenge, and reflect on the king's justice and the God who searches the human spirit.
20.lookfor: Look for the market scene of the haggling buyer, the questions about who can know his own heart, and the image of the lamp.

insights.title: Like the watercourses
insights.body: The king's heart is in Yahweh's hand like the watercourses, turned wherever he desires (21:1). Farmers in Egypt and Mesopotamia directed irrigation water by opening and closing small channels. Even the most powerful king is like water a gardener steers. Ezra says God turned the heart of a Persian king to help Israel.

insights.title: Better than sacrifice
insights.body: To do righteousness and justice is more acceptable to Yahweh than sacrifice (21:3). This agrees with Samuel's to obey is better than sacrifice and with Hosea's I desire mercy, and not sacrifice, which Jesus quotes.

insights.title: The corner of the housetop
insights.body: It is better to live in a corner of the housetop than with a contentious woman (21:9), and better a desert land (21:19). Israelite houses had flat roofs used for storage, work and sometimes sleeping. A corner up there was cramped and exposed, but at least quiet.

insights.title: The cry of the poor
insights.body: Whoever stops his ears at the cry of the poor will cry out and not be heard (21:13). The saying is about reciprocity with God. Jesus' story of the rich man and Lazarus turns on a rich man who ignored a beggar at his gate.

insights.title: The wicked as ransom
insights.body: The wicked is a ransom for the righteous (21:18). The idea is that the trouble the wicked plan for others falls on themselves instead. Haman, hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai, is a classic biblical example.

insights.title: The scoffer named
insights.body: The proud and haughty man's name is scoffer (21:24). The scoffer, or mocker, is the worst kind of fool in Proverbs: not just ignorant but contemptuous of correction. The book gives him up as hopeless, as in the line that rebuking him only invites insult.

insights.title: Victory is with Yahweh
insights.body: "The horse is prepared for the day of battle; but victory is with Yahweh" (21:31). Horses and chariots were the most advanced military power of the day. Preparation is wise, but the outcome belongs to God, the same balance found in Psalm 20.

insights.title: No wisdom against Yahweh
insights.body: There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against Yahweh (21:30). The verse comes just after many sayings praising wisdom. What does it mean that even the best human wisdom has a limit?

21.summary: These sayings declare God's control even over kings, prize justice above sacrifice, warn about greed, pride and laziness, and end by saying no wisdom can succeed against Yahweh.
21.lookfor: Notice the image of the king's heart as water, the two sayings about escaping a quarrelsome home, and the horse at the end.

insights.title: A good name
insights.body: "A good name is more desirable than great riches" (22:1). A person's name stood for his reputation and character, which outlast possessions. Ecclesiastes adds that a good name is better than fine perfume.

insights.title: The rich and poor alike
insights.body: The rich and the poor have this in common: Yahweh is the maker of them all (22:2). The verse does not deny that wealth gives power (22:7). It reminds both rich and poor that they stand before the same Creator.

insights.title: Train up a child
insights.body: "Train up a child in the way he should go, and when he is old he will not depart from it" (22:6). The Hebrew says literally according to his way, which may mean the right way or a way suited to the child. Like most proverbs it states what generally happens, not a guarantee, and should not be used to blame parents of children who stray.

insights.title: A lion in the street
insights.body: The sluggard says there is a lion outside and he will be killed in the streets (22:13). Lions did live in Israel, but not in city streets. The excuse is absurd, which is the point: laziness invents dangers to avoid work.

insights.title: Thirty sayings
insights.body: At 22:17 a new heading introduces the words of the wise, and 22:20 refers to thirty excellent things. In 1923 an Egyptian text called the Instruction of Amenemope, which has thirty chapters, was published, and scholars noticed close parallels with 22:17 to 23:11. Most think the Israelite sage adapted Egyptian wisdom, reshaping it around trust in Yahweh (22:19).

insights.title: The ancient boundary stone
insights.body: Don't move the ancient boundary stone (22:28). Amenemope has a similar warning. In both cultures moving a field marker was a quiet way to steal land, especially from widows and orphans, and Israel's law and prophets condemn it.

insights.title: Yahweh pleads their case
insights.body: Don't crush the needy in court, for Yahweh will plead their case (22:22-23). The court was held at the city gate, where the powerful could bend justice. Proverbs names God himself as the poor man's advocate.

insights.title: Skilled in his work
insights.body: A man skilled in his work will serve kings (22:29). Amenemope ends with a similar claim about the skilled scribe. What does it suggest that the Bible honours skill and craftsmanship as part of wisdom?

22.summary: The last of Solomon's sayings praise a good name and humility, warn about debt and the oppression of the poor, and then a new section begins with thirty sayings of the wise.
22.lookfor: Notice where the voice changes at verse 17, the reference to thirty sayings, and the warning about the ancient boundary stone.

insights.title: Dining with a ruler
insights.body: When you eat with a ruler, consider carefully what is before you and put a knife to your throat if you are greedy (23:1-2). Egyptian instruction texts give similar advice to young officials invited to a great man's table. The danger is that his delicacies are deceitful food (23:3), offered to win influence.

insights.title: Riches with wings
insights.body: Wealth sprouts wings like an eagle and flies into the sky (23:5). The Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope has a strikingly similar line about riches making themselves wings like geese and flying to heaven. It is one of the clearest parallels between the two texts.

insights.title: Their strong Defender
insights.body: Don't encroach on the fields of the fatherless, for their Defender is strong (23:10-11). The Hebrew is go'el, the kinsman-redeemer who bought back land and protected vulnerable relatives, as Boaz did for Ruth. Orphans with no human go'el have God himself.

insights.title: The rod and Sheol
insights.body: Punish him with the rod, and save his soul from Sheol (23:14). The saying assumes the ancient practice of physical discipline, and says a child will not die from correction but may die from its absence. Readers today differ on how literally to apply it, but the aim it names is the child's life.

insights.title: Glutton and drunkard
insights.body: Don't be among heavy drinkers and gluttons, for they become poor (23:20-21). The same pair describes the rebellious son in Deuteronomy, and Jesus' critics used it against him because he ate with sinners.

insights.title: Buy the truth
insights.body: Buy the truth, and don't sell it (23:23). As in chapter 4, wisdom is pictured as something worth any price to get and too valuable ever to trade away.

insights.title: Who has woe
insights.body: The poem on wine (23:29-35) opens with six questions, then answers: those who linger over mixed wine. It ends in the drunkard's own words, unable to feel his bruises and already looking for another drink (23:35). It is one of the most vivid portraits of addiction in ancient literature.

insights.title: Give me your heart
insights.body: "My son, give me your heart" (23:26). The father asks for more than obedience. What is the difference between following rules and handing over one's heart?

23.summary: The sayings of the wise continue with advice on table manners before rulers, the fleeting nature of riches, protecting orphans' fields, disciplining children, and a vivid portrait of the drunkard.
23.lookfor: Watch for riches that grow wings, the strong Defender of the fatherless, and the series of questions that opens the poem on wine.

insights.title: Built by wisdom
insights.body: Through wisdom a house is built, and by knowledge its rooms are filled with treasure (24:3-4). This echoes Wisdom building her house in chapter 9 and the wise woman building hers in chapter 14. The house can mean the building, the family and the household's wealth.

insights.title: Rescue the doomed
insights.body: Rescue those being led away to death (24:11). The excuse we didn't know is answered with a question: doesn't he who weighs the hearts know (24:12)? The saying leaves no room for convenient ignorance when others are in danger.

insights.title: Seven falls
insights.body: A righteous man falls seven times and rises up again (24:16). Seven means many. The righteous are not people who never stumble, but people who keep getting up, while the wicked stay down.

insights.title: Don't gloat
insights.body: Don't rejoice when your enemy falls (24:17). The reason given, lest Yahweh turn away his wrath from him (24:18), is surprising, but the command itself goes beyond merely not seeking revenge. Job counts not gloating over an enemy as part of his integrity, and Jesus calls for love of enemies.

insights.title: Fear God and the king
insights.body: My son, fear Yahweh and the king (24:21). Peter's Fear God. Honor the king echoes this verse. Wisdom literature counted respect for lawful authority as part of an ordered life under God.

insights.title: A kiss on the lips
insights.body: An honest answer is like a kiss on the lips (24:26). A kiss was a sign of friendship and loyalty between friends and family. A straight answer, even an unwelcome one, is a mark of true friendship.

insights.title: Not as he did to me
insights.body: Don't say, "I will do to him as he has done to me" (24:29). The law's eye for eye set limits for courts, but this saying forbids personal tit-for-tat, anticipating Jesus' teaching about turning the other cheek.

insights.title: A lesson from a field
insights.body: The speaker passes the sluggard's vineyard, overgrown with thorns and its wall broken down (24:30-31). He considers and learns (24:32), and the lesson is the same as in chapter 6: a little sleep leads to poverty. Wisdom grows from paying attention to ordinary things.

24.summary: The sayings of the wise warn against envying evildoers, urge rescuing those led to death, forbid gloating over an enemy's fall, and end with a short look at the sluggard's ruined field.
24.lookfor: Notice the call to rescue the doomed, the righteous man who falls seven times, and what the observer learns from the overgrown vineyard.

names.name: Hezekiah
names.gloss: A king of Judah around 715 to 686 BC known for his religious reforms.

insights.title: Copied by Hezekiah's men
insights.body: The heading says Hezekiah's men copied out these proverbs (25:1). Hezekiah's reign saw religious reform and a revival of temple music and writings, and many scholars think his court scribes collected and edited older material. It is a rare glimpse of how biblical books were gathered.

insights.title: Concealing and searching
insights.body: It is God's glory to conceal a thing and the king's glory to search it out (25:2). God's world holds mysteries, and wise rulers investigate them. Francis Bacon quoted it in defence of scientific enquiry.

insights.title: Come up here
insights.body: Don't claim a place among great men; it is better to be told come up here than be sent lower (25:6-7). Jesus tells a parable at a dinner with almost the same advice about the seats at a wedding feast.

insights.title: Apples of gold
insights.body: "A word fitly spoken is like apples of gold in settings of silver" (25:11). The fruit may be apples, apricots or another golden fruit, and the image may be jewellery or carved decoration. Either way, it is a precious thing in a beautiful setting, like the right word at the right moment.

insights.title: Snow at harvest
insights.body: A faithful messenger is like the cold of snow in the time of harvest (25:13). Snow at harvest would ruin crops (26:1), so the image is probably of a cool drink chilled with snow brought from the mountains. In the heat of harvest, it refreshes.

insights.title: Coals of fire
insights.body: If your enemy is hungry, feed him, for you will heap coals of fire on his head (25:21-22). Paul quotes this verse in Romans. Interpreters debate the image: it may mean the burning shame that leads an enemy to repent, and some point to an Egyptian ritual in which a penitent carried coals on his head.

insights.title: A puzzling north wind
insights.body: The north wind produces rain (25:23). In Israel the rain usually comes from the west off the Mediterranean, and the north wind is generally cold and dry. Some suggest the saying came from elsewhere, or that north here means north-west.

insights.title: A city without walls
insights.body: Like a city that is broken down and without walls is a man without self-control (25:28). Walls were a city's only defence. What kind of attacks is a person without self-restraint left open to?

25.summary: A new collection of Solomon's proverbs copied by Hezekiah's scribes opens with sayings about kings and courts, and moves on to vivid comparisons about timely words, patience, and kindness to enemies.
25.lookfor: Look for the comparisons that begin with like and as, the golden apples, and the advice about feeding an enemy.

insights.title: Nothing fits a fool
insights.body: Honour fits a fool like snow in summer or rain in harvest (26:1). Verses 1 to 12 form a cluster about fools, and verses 13 to 16 one about sluggards. Each comparison is short, memorable and often funny.

insights.title: Answer him, don't answer him
insights.body: "Don't answer a fool according to his folly" (26:4) is followed at once by "Answer a fool according to his folly" (26:5). The Talmud records rabbis troubled by the contradiction, who resolved it by applying the sayings to different situations. Placed side by side, they teach that wisdom lies in knowing which proverb fits the moment.

insights.title: The undeserved curse
insights.body: An undeserved curse doesn't come to rest, like a fluttering sparrow (26:2). Ancient people widely believed spoken curses had power. Proverbs says a curse without cause has nowhere to land.

insights.title: Like a dog to vomit
insights.body: "As a dog that returns to his vomit, so is a fool who repeats his folly" (26:11). Peter quotes this proverb to describe those who return to their old ways after knowing the way of righteousness. Dogs in Israel were mostly scavengers, not pets, which makes the image even more unpleasant.

insights.title: Worse than a fool
insights.body: Do you see a man wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him (26:12). After eleven verses about fools, the cluster turns on the reader. Thinking oneself wise is worse than open folly.

insights.title: Grabbing a dog's ears
insights.body: Meddling in someone else's quarrel is like grabbing a dog by the ears (26:17). The dogs of the ancient Near East were half-wild, so the picture is of someone who will certainly be bitten and cannot let go.

insights.title: Silver dross on clay
insights.body: Fervent lips over an evil heart are like silver dross on an earthen vessel (26:23). Many scholars, comparing a word in Ugaritic, read like glaze on a pot: a shiny surface over cheap clay. It is a picture of hypocrisy similar to Jesus' whitened tombs.

insights.title: Only joking
insights.body: A man who deceives his neighbour and says, "Am I not joking?" is like a madman shooting deadly arrows (26:18-19). Why might deception disguised as a joke be singled out as so dangerous?

26.summary: These sayings mock the fool, the sluggard and the troublemaker in a series of sharp comparisons, ending with warnings about gossip, deceit and flattery.
26.lookfor: Notice the clusters on fools, then sluggards, then gossips and liars, and the two sayings about answering a fool that seem to contradict each other.

insights.title: Don't boast about tomorrow
insights.body: "Don't boast about tomorrow; for you don't know what a day may bring" (27:1). James expands this into his warning to merchants who plan a year's trade, reminding them their life is a vapour.

insights.title: Wounds and kisses
insights.body: Faithful are the wounds of a friend, while an enemy's kisses are profuse (27:6). A friend's honest criticism helps, and lavish affection can hide betrayal. Christian readers often recall Judas betraying Jesus with a kiss.

insights.title: A neighbour near
insights.body: Better a neighbour who is near than a distant brother (27:10). In a world where family was everything, this is a surprising saying. Practical help in a crisis comes from those close at hand.

insights.title: Iron sharpens iron
insights.body: "Iron sharpens iron; so a man sharpens his friend's countenance" (27:17). Iron tools and weapons became common in Israel during the monarchy, and blades were sharpened against harder metal or stone. Friends make each other sharper through honest exchange.

insights.title: Never satisfied
insights.body: Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied, and neither are human eyes (27:20). The grave keeps receiving the dead, and human desire keeps wanting more. Ecclesiastes says the same of the eye and the ear.

insights.title: Refined by praise
insights.body: The crucible is for silver and the furnace for gold, but man is refined by his praise (27:21). The Hebrew is compressed: a person is tested by how he handles praise, or by what he praises. Success can reveal character as much as hardship.

insights.title: Know your flocks
insights.body: The chapter ends with a five-verse poem telling the reader to know the state of his flocks (27:23-27). Riches and even a crown do not last, but well-tended animals renew themselves each year, giving wool, milk and money for land. Many think it was addressed to rulers, reminding them that stewardship outlasts status.

insights.title: A heart in the water
insights.body: Like water reflects a face, so a man's heart reflects the man (27:19). Does this mean we come to know ourselves by looking at our own hearts, or by seeing ourselves in others? Both readings have been held.

27.summary: These sayings warn against boasting about tomorrow, prize honest friends who wound and sharpen, observe the restlessness of human desire, and close with a short poem on caring for flocks.
27.lookfor: Look for the friend's wounds and the enemy's kisses, iron sharpening iron, and the change to a shepherd's advice at the end.

insights.title: Fleeing when no one pursues
insights.body: "The wicked flee when no one pursues; but the righteous are as bold as a lion" (28:1). Leviticus warns that the disobedient will flee when no one pursues. A guilty conscience creates its own enemies.

insights.title: Torah in the gates
insights.body: Chapters 28 and 29 mention the law, torah, more often than any other part of the sayings (28:4, 28:7, 28:9, 29:18). Scholars debate whether it means the law of Moses or the teaching of the wise. The two may not have been far apart in the minds of those who collected the book.

insights.title: Interest on loans
insights.body: He who increases wealth by excessive interest gathers it for one who will be kind to the poor (28:8). The law forbade lending at interest to fellow Israelites, especially to the poor. In practice, high-interest loans drove many farmers into debt slavery.

insights.title: Confess and find mercy
insights.body: "He who conceals his sins doesn't prosper, but whoever confesses and renounces them finds mercy" (28:13). This is one of the clearest statements of repentance in Proverbs. Psalm 32 describes the same experience, and John promises forgiveness to those who confess.

insights.title: Lions and bears
insights.body: A wicked ruler over helpless people is like a roaring lion or a charging bear (28:15). Several sayings in this chapter and the next look at what happens to ordinary people when rulers are wicked: people hide themselves (28:12, 28:28).

insights.title: Rulers rise and fall
insights.body: Four sayings about the righteous and wicked coming to power (28:12, 28:28, 29:2, 29:16) seem to mark out sections in chapters 28 and 29. Many think these chapters were shaped for training young men for government service.

insights.title: Partiality for bread
insights.body: To show partiality is not good, yet a man will do wrong for a piece of bread (28:21). Corruption often happens for very small rewards. The saying is realistic about how cheaply justice can be sold.

insights.title: Blessed is the one who fears
insights.body: Blessed is the man who always fears (28:14). Fear here is probably reverent caution about sin, set against hardening the heart. How can constant fear be called blessed?

28.summary: These sayings contrast the righteous and wicked under bad and good rulers, value keeping the law, warn against dishonest gain and partiality, and promise mercy to the one who confesses.
28.lookfor: Notice how often the law is mentioned, the sayings about rulers who oppress, and the verse about hiding and confessing sins.

insights.title: A stiff neck
insights.body: He who is often rebuked and stiffens his neck will be destroyed suddenly (29:1). Stiff-necked is the word used of Israel in the wilderness. A refusal to listen eventually becomes beyond remedy.

insights.title: Justice and the throne
insights.body: The king by justice makes the land stable (29:4), and the king who judges the poor fairly will have his throne established forever (29:14). Israel's ideal king defends the weak, a hope that the prophets attached to the coming son of David.

insights.title: Both given sight
insights.body: The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: Yahweh gives sight to both (29:13). Oppressors and oppressed alike owe their life to God, which is both a comfort to the poor and a warning to the oppressor.

insights.title: Where there is no revelation
insights.body: Where there is no revelation, the people cast off restraint (29:18). The word chazon means prophetic vision, God's word to a prophet. The famous older rendering about vision is often used of leadership plans, but the Hebrew is about the loss of God's word, as the second line about keeping the law shows.

insights.title: The fear of man
insights.body: "The fear of man proves to be a snare, but whoever puts his trust in Yahweh is kept safe" (29:25). Fearing what others think traps a person into compromise. The Bible repeatedly sets fear of people against trust in God.

insights.title: Courting the ruler
insights.body: Many seek the ruler's favour, but a man's justice comes from Yahweh (29:26). Petitioners crowded royal courts seeking favourable judgments. Final justice, Proverbs says, is not in the king's hands but in God's.

insights.title: Hasty words
insights.body: A man who is hasty in his words has less hope than a fool (29:20). The same verdict was given in chapter 26 about the man wise in his own eyes. Quick speech and self-satisfaction are treated as worse than ordinary folly.

insights.title: Mutual detesting
insights.body: The collection ends: the dishonest detest the righteous, and the upright detest the wicked (29:27). Is this simply realism about two ways of life that cannot be at ease together, or does it say something about how the righteous should feel about evil?

29.summary: The last sayings of Hezekiah's collection look at rulers and justice, correction and pride, and the need for revelation, ending with the righteous and wicked detesting one another.
29.lookfor: Look for the verse about revelation, the comparison between fearing people and trusting Yahweh, and the final contrast.

names.name: Agur
names.gloss: The otherwise unknown author of this chapter, probably not an Israelite.

names.name: Ithiel
names.gloss: One of the men addressed in 30:1, though the Hebrew may be a phrase rather than a name.

names.name: Ucal
names.gloss: Another addressee, perhaps also a phrase rather than a name.

insights.title: Who was Agur?
insights.body: Agur son of Jakeh appears nowhere else. The word translated revelation (30:1), massa, may instead name Massa, an Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael, so Agur may have been a non-Israelite sage. With different vowels, Ithiel and Ucal can be read as I am weary, O God, and worn out.

insights.title: Who has ascended?
insights.body: Agur's questions (30:4) recall God's challenge to Job: who has gathered the wind, bound the waters, established the ends of the earth? What is his name, and his son's name? Christians have heard a hint of the Son in the last question, and John speaks of the Son of Man who ascended and descended.

insights.title: Every word flawless
insights.body: Every word of God is flawless; he is a shield to those who take refuge in him (30:5). This closely follows Psalm 18. The warning not to add to his words (30:6) recalls Deuteronomy and the end of Revelation.

insights.title: Neither poverty nor riches
insights.body: Agur's prayer, the only one in Proverbs, asks for neither poverty nor riches, only the food that is needful (30:8). Wealth can lead to forgetting God and poverty to stealing (30:9). It is close to the Lord's Prayer's daily bread.

insights.title: Three things, four
insights.body: Agur uses the numerical pattern x and x plus one (30:15, 30:18, 30:21, 30:29). The last item in each list is the climax: the way of a man with a maiden (30:19), the servant who becomes heir to her mistress (30:23).

insights.title: Little but wise
insights.body: Four small creatures are exceedingly wise: ants, conies, locusts and lizards (30:24-28). The conies are rock hyraxes, small animals that live among the rocks of Israel. A lizard, easily caught by hand, still gets into kings' palaces.

insights.title: The greyhound
insights.body: Among the stately walkers is the greyhound (30:31), but the Hebrew, literally girded of loins, is uncertain. Ancient translations suggest a rooster strutting among hens or a war horse.

insights.title: Agur's humility
insights.body: Agur calls himself the most ignorant of men (30:2) and then speaks with great wisdom. Is his confession of ignorance the beginning of his wisdom?

30.summary: Agur confesses his ignorance before the Creator, prays for neither poverty nor riches, and offers a series of numerical sayings about things never satisfied, too wonderful to understand, small but wise and stately in their going.
30.lookfor: Notice Agur's questions about who made the world, his short prayer, and the patterns of three things and four.

names.name: Lemuel
names.gloss: A king otherwise unknown, perhaps from the Arabian tribe of Massa.

insights.title: A mother's counsel
insights.body: The words of King Lemuel come from his mother's teaching (31:1). Queen mothers had real influence in ancient courts, as Bathsheba did with Solomon. Jewish tradition identified Lemuel with Solomon and his mother with Bathsheba, though many scholars think he was a non-Israelite king.

insights.title: Wine for the perishing
insights.body: Give strong drink to him who is ready to perish (31:6). A king must stay sober to judge fairly (31:4-5), but wine could ease the suffering of the dying. The Talmud links this verse to a Jerusalem custom of giving drugged wine to the condemned, which may lie behind the wine mixed with myrrh offered to Jesus.

insights.title: Open your mouth
insights.body: Open your mouth for the mute, in the cause of all who are left desolate (31:8-9). The king's first duty is to speak and judge for those who cannot defend themselves. These verses are often quoted in calls for social justice.

insights.title: A woman of valour
insights.body: The poem (31:10-31) is an acrostic: each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Its subject is the eshet chayil, a woman of strength or valour; chayil elsewhere describes warriors and wealth. Jewish households traditionally sing this poem at the Sabbath table on Friday evening.

insights.title: A working household
insights.body: She buys wool and flax, spins with distaff and spindle (31:19), buys a field and plants a vineyard (31:16), and sells garments to merchants (31:24). The poem shows a woman running a large household enterprise. Her husband is respected at the city gates, where the elders sat, partly because of her (31:23).

insights.title: Ruth the worthy woman
insights.body: In some Hebrew manuscripts, including the Leningrad Codex, the book of Ruth comes right after Proverbs, and Boaz calls Ruth a worthy woman, the same phrase as 31:10. Ruth, a poor foreign widow, shows that this praise is about character and faithfulness, not wealth or status.

insights.title: The fear of Yahweh at the end
insights.body: "Charm is deceitful, and beauty is vain; but a woman who fears Yahweh, she shall be praised" (31:30). The book that began with the fear of Yahweh as the beginning of knowledge ends with a woman who embodies it. Many scholars see her as Lady Wisdom from chapters 1 to 9 at home in real life.

insights.title: An ideal or a portrait?
insights.body: Some readers take the poem as a description of one real woman, others as an ideal no one fully matches, others as wisdom itself in human form. How does each reading change what the poem asks of its readers, men as well as women?

31.summary: King Lemuel records his mother's advice to rule justly and avoid women and wine that destroy kings, and the book ends with an alphabet poem praising the valiant wife who fears Yahweh.
31.lookfor: Watch for whose words these are, the call to speak up for those who cannot, and what the capable wife actually does through the day.

intro.who: The headings credit Solomon (1:1, 10:1, 25:1), but the book also names other sources: the sayings of the wise, the men of King Hezekiah, Agur and King Lemuel. Jewish tradition in the Talmud links the book's final form to Hezekiah and his company, and most modern scholars see it as a collection of collections gathered by Israel's scribes and teachers over several centuries.
intro.when: Solomon reigned around 970 to 930 BC and Hezekiah around 715 to 686 BC. Many scholars think chapters 1 to 9 were written last and that the book reached its present shape after the exile, perhaps in the Persian period, though others date most of it to the monarchy.
intro.why: It trains the young, and anyone willing to learn, in practical wisdom for ordinary life (speech, work, money, family, friendship and power) rooted in the fear of Yahweh. Like other wisdom books of the ancient Near East it teaches through sharp observation, but it ties every skill for living to knowing Israel's God.
